posts.title: Aizawa’s round shell with a hole through it
posts.excerpt: The Aizawa attractor fills a ball-like shell with a funnel down the middle: six ODE knobs and a cool-to-warm trail on Classical Chaos, ported from the old CanvasWorld workshop.

posts.title: Why the Lorenz attractor never closes
posts.excerpt: Why the Lorenz butterfly never settles into a loop, and how Classical Chaos draws that trail with three ODEs and a simple Euler step.

posts.title: Four Hopalong variants, side by side
posts.excerpt: Barry Martin’s 1981 Hopalong map (the Skull attractor) in four live Classical Chaos variants — classic, positive, additive, sinusoidal — so you can see what changes when the rule changes.

posts.title: Clifford’s sine–cosine cloud
posts.excerpt: Clifford Pickover’s 2D map: four knobs, sine and cosine of crossed terms, and a purple point cloud that reshapes when you nudge a, b, c, or d.

posts.title: Escape time: how the Mandelbrot boundary gets drawn on Classical Chaos
posts.excerpt: The Mandelbrot boundary keeps revealing more detail under zoom. Classical Chaos paints each pixel by how many steps the repeating z² + c run takes to blow past a fixed bound.

posts.title: Watching holes open in the Sierpiński gasket
posts.excerpt: Sierpiński’s gasket: cut the middle out of a triangle, then out of every leftover corner. Classical Chaos grows that lace live as depth climbs.

posts.title: Bedhead attractor: the mint map cloud
posts.excerpt: The Bedhead attractor is a 2D iterated map: seed, short formula, next (x, y), until a mint-green cloud piles up. Classical Chaos draws it from defaults near a ≈ 0.65, b ≈ 0.73.

posts.title: Bogdanov Map: a cloud that reshapes with a, b, and μ
posts.excerpt: The Bogdanov Map is a discrete 2D chaotic map: a seed and a short rule pile into a colored cloud. Twist a, b, and μ on Classical Chaos and the same seed wears a different silhouette.

posts.title: Brusselator: a chemical oscillator as a phase-plane trail
posts.excerpt: The Brusselator is a theoretical chemical oscillator: two concentrations chase a closed cycle in the phase plane. Classical Chaos draws that orbit as a live trail.

posts.title: Fractal Dream: four sines, one folded cloud
posts.excerpt: Fractal Dream is a 2D iterated map: four sines of crossed terms pile points into a folded cloud. Classical Chaos starts at (−2, −2) with a, b, c, d in [0, 3].

posts.title: Gumowski–Mira: a soft bump named G
posts.excerpt: Gumowski–Mira is a discrete 2D map with a helper G that mixes linear and rational pieces. Classical Chaos defaults sit near a = 0.008, b = 0.05, μ = −0.9, seed (0, 0.5).

posts.title: Hénon map: the classic 1976 crescent
posts.excerpt: Michel Hénon’s 1976 map packs a folded crescent into two updates. Classical Chaos iterates the classic form: x′ = 1 − a x² + y, y′ = b x, with a = 1.4, b = 0.3.

posts.title: Gingerbread Man: absolute value, cookie silhouette
posts.excerpt: Devaney’s Gingerbread Man is a fixed 2D map: absolute value folds the plane until a cookie silhouette piles up. Classical Chaos draws it from (−0.1, 0) with the classic formula locked.

posts.title: Ikeda map: one knob named a
posts.excerpt: Kensuke Ikeda’s 1979 discrete map: rotate and scale a 2D point until a folded cloud piles up. Classical Chaos uses parameter a (default 1), with a chaos band around [0.6, 1].

posts.title: Julia sets: one fixed c, a whole plane of starting points
posts.excerpt: Fix one complex c and ask which starting z stay bounded under z² + c. Classical Chaos paints each pixel by how fast that orbit escapes.

posts.title: Calabi–Yau: a Fermat slice as a coral wire
posts.excerpt: String-theory posters love the Calabi–Yau name. Classical Chaos draws a Hanson slice of a Fermat surface as a growing particle wire — coral to amber to teal — not the full six-real-dimensional 3-fold.

posts.title: Schoen’s gyroid: a labyrinth that tiles space
posts.excerpt: Alan Schoen’s gyroid is a two-sided labyrinth that repeats on a cubic lattice. Classical Chaos draws a trigonometric level set as a coral-to-teal point cloud that grows in over time.

posts.title: Barth’s sextic: where did those icosahedral spikes come from?
posts.excerpt: Wolf Barth’s 1996 sextic is a degree-6 algebraic surface with icosahedral symmetry and dozens of pinch points. Classical Chaos draws it as a coral-to-teal particle cloud on the isosurface.

posts.title: Schwarz P: a labyrinth that tiles the cube
posts.excerpt: Schwarz’s primitive (P) surface is a two-sided labyrinth on a cubic lattice — a TPMS cousin of the gyroid. Classical Chaos grows a coral–amber–teal particle wire of a trig approximation.

posts.title: Dini surface: tractrix helicoid with constant negative curvature
posts.excerpt: Ulisse Dini’s 1866 surface is the helicoid of a tractrix: a pseudospherical band that climbs when twist turns on. Classical Chaos draws it as a coral-to-teal UV particle wire.

posts.title: Roman surface: Steiner’s self-crossing RP²
posts.excerpt: Four lobes that slide through each other: Steiner’s Roman surface (real projective plane in 3D). Classical Chaos draws the UV wire; squash lives on the full canvas.

posts.title: Enneper surface: a minimal sheet that crosses itself
posts.excerpt: Alfred Enneper’s 1864 minimal surface has mean curvature zero and a short polynomial map — and once the UV patch is large enough, the sheet crosses through itself. Classical Chaos draws that cage as a UV particle wire.

posts.title: Boy surface: the immersion that has to cross
posts.excerpt: Boy surface crosses itself in 3D: Werner Boy’s 1901 immersion of the real projective plane, with a triple point and no clean outside. Classical Chaos draws it as a polar isoline wire that grows in.
